examples: The defense argued that the search had been illegal from the start.
Economists argue that the credit mostly benefits people who would have bought anyway.
She argued for a small pilot before anyone committed to a full rollout.
They spent an hour arguing about whether the deposit was refundable.
Nobody argued that the old system was better — only that it was cheaper.
He argued against moving the deadline, and the committee overruled him.
She argued him out of resigning, and he stayed another four years.
It has long been argued that the tax pays for itself, and it has never been shown.
entries.русский: утверждать, доказывать — выдвигать позицию с доводами; с предлогом — спорить
entries.type: reporting verb — reasoned claim
entries.patterns: argue + that-clause · argue + for / against + noun phrase · argue + for / against + -ing · argue + about / over + noun phrase · argue + about / over + wh-clause · argue + with + person · argue + sb + into / out of + -ing · argue + noun phrase (argue a case, argue the point) · passive it is argued that
entries.never: argue someone to do something and argue someone that — argue takes no personal object in front of a clause. The verb for talking a person into something is persuade or convince: He argued that we should wait ✓ / He persuaded us to wait ✓ / He argued us to wait ✗. The one genuine personal-object frame is argue + sb + into / out of + -ing, and it reports persuasion rather than a claim: She argued him out of resigning ✓. And no bare question clause — argue why the plan would fail ✗, argue whether to go ✗ — the question has to ride in on a preposition: argued about why the plan would fail ✓, argued over whether to go ✓.
entries.reports: a position put forward with reasons attached to it. Claim signals the reporter's doubt and prove concedes the case; argue is neutral on whether the reasoning worked, reporting only that reasoning was offered.
entries.see also: reason, conclude, point out, prove, demonstrate

examples: The nurse asked whether I had eaten anything since midnight.
He asked me why the invoice was two hundred dollars short.
She asked to see the manager, and then asked the manager for a refund.
Somebody in the back asked how long the recording would stay up.
I asked about the deposit twice and never got a straight answer.
Don't ask me what he meant by that.
The witness was asked to remain in the building until the hearing ended.
She asked the front desk for a later checkout and got it.
entries.русский: спросить; попросить — нейтральный глагол вопроса, а с инфинитивом — просьба (ask to do)
entries.register: neutral; the default verb for reporting any question
entries.type: reporting verb — question, and with an infinitive a request
entries.patterns: ask + wh-clause · ask + if / whether-clause · ask + sb + wh-clause · ask + sb + if / whether-clause · ask + noun phrase (ask a question) · ask + sb + noun phrase (ask me a favor) · ask + to-infinitive (ask to leave — you want to act) · ask + sb + to-infinitive (ask me to leave — you want them to act) · ask + that-clause + subjunctive (formal request) · ask + for + noun phrase · ask + sb + for + noun phrase · ask + about / after + noun phrase · ask + wh-word + to-infinitive · ask + direct quotation, as a quotative tag ("Where do you live?" she asked) · passive be asked to do something
entries.never: ask to someone whether — the person goes straight after the verb with no preposition: She asked me whether I was free, never She asked to me whether. And never keep question word order inside the clause: He asked where was I ✗ → He asked where I was ✓. Ask takes no -ing complement — ask leaving early ✗ → She asked to leave early ✓ — and it cannot take a that-clause in the question sense: ask that she was free ✗ → She asked whether she was free ✓. Ask that is always a request, and then it takes the subjunctive (She asked that the room be cleared), never a question.
entries.reports: a question actually spoken. It is the unmarked choice, carrying no formality (inquire), no impatience (demand to know), and no doubt about the answer (query).
entries.see also: inquire, wonder, want to know, query, question, Reported questions, Requests: the ask family

examples: I assumed the meeting was still on, since nobody said otherwise.
The estimate assumes that materials arrive by the first of the month.
She wrongly assumed the fee covered parking.
Let's not assume he saw the email — it's easy to miss.
The report assumed the plant to be operating at full capacity.
It is generally assumed that the two cases are related.
"Is the deal still on?" — "I assume so, but nobody has confirmed it."
entries.pronunciation note: American English drops the y glide; British uh-SYOOM
entries.русский: предполагать, исходить из того что — принять без проверки (в отличие от conclude)
entries.type: reporting verb — belief taken for granted
entries.patterns: assume + that-clause · assume + sb/sth + to-infinitive, nearly always to be (formal: assumed him to be the owner) · assume + noun phrase · assume + so / not · passive it is assumed that · passive sb is assumed to be
entries.never: assume me that and assume to someone that — no personal object and no to-phrase for the hearer, because assume reports a private belief rather than something said to anybody. Assume also takes no wh-clause and no -ing: assume where he had gone ✗ and assume him going ✗ → I assumed he had gone home ✓ or I guessed where he had gone ✓.
entries.reports: a belief adopted without checking it. That is the judgment the word carries: conclude implies evidence was weighed, assume implies it was skipped, which is why You assumed I'd say yes is a complaint and You concluded I'd say yes is not.
entries.see also: suppose, gather, believe, think, infer, conclude

examples: I believe the office closes at four on Fridays.
Investigators believe the fire started in the crawl space.
She didn't believe a word of it.
The painting is believed to be a copy made around 1810.
We have no reason to believe that anyone else was involved.
Do you believe he actually said that?
She believes in saying exactly what she means, which has cost her more than one client.
It is widely believed that the two companies had already agreed on a price.
entries.русский: считать, полагать — держать за истину без прямого знания; осторожнее и книжнее, чем think
entries.register: neutral to formal; slightly more careful than think
entries.type: reporting verb — belief, often hedged
entries.patterns: believe + that-clause · believe + sb/sth + to-infinitive (formal) · believe + noun phrase (believe her, believe the story) · believe + in + noun phrase · believe + in + -ing · believe so / believe not · passive sb is believed to be · passive it is believed that
entries.never: believe to me that and believe me that the door was locked — believe me means "trust what I say," so it cannot double as the hearer slot of a report; the repair is told me the door was locked ✓. Believe also takes no wh-clause and no bare -ing: believe where he went ✗, believe him lying ✗ → I believe he is lying ✓.
entries.reports: something held to be true without direct knowledge of it. Against know, it concedes the possibility of error; against think, it is a touch more formal and more committed, which is why news writing uses is believed to be and not is thought to be when it wants to sound careful.
entries.see also: think, suppose, understand, gather, assume

examples: She calculated that the detour would cost them forty minutes.
The actuary calculated how much the policy would pay out over thirty years.
He calculated the total in his head and came up two dollars short.
The city calculates its water rates on a sliding scale.
Nobody had calculated what the overtime would do to the budget.
The insult was calculated to land in front of an audience.
entries.русский: подсчитать, вычислить — получить цифру или вывод расчётом (ср. estimate — «прикинуть»)
entries.type: reporting verb — conclusion reached by figuring
entries.patterns: calculate + that-clause · calculate + wh-clause · calculate + noun phrase · calculate + noun phrase + at + amount · passive it is calculated that · passive be calculated to (= designed to)
entries.never: calculate someone that and calculate me the total — no personal object in either slot; if you need a hearer at all, use for: calculated the total for me ✓. And keep the two to-forms apart: be calculated to means "designed to produce an effect" (a remark calculated to offend), not "worked out that" — He calculated the trip to take four hours ✗ → He calculated that the trip would take four hours ✓.
entries.reports: a figure or a judgment arrived at by working something out, spoken aloud. Estimate admits the number is approximate; calculate claims it was derived.
entries.see also: estimate, conclude, reckon, figure, predict

examples: She cited three studies, none of which said what she claimed.
The judge cited an 1897 ruling that nobody in the room had read.
He turned down the offer, citing the commute.
The article cites an anonymous source close to the negotiations.
Both reports cite the same faulty sensor as the cause.
You have to cite every source you paraphrase, not just the ones you quote.
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of site and sight
entries.русский: ссылаться на, приводить — офиц./юр.: назвать источник или причину, а не сами слова
entries.register: formal; standard in journalism, law, and academic writing
entries.type: reporting verb — attributed source or reason
entries.patterns: cite + noun phrase · cite + noun phrase + as + noun phrase (cited the ruling as precedent) · cite + sb + as saying (+ that-clause) · cite + noun phrase + for + noun phrase (= issue a citation: cited him for speeding) · cite + noun phrase + in support of / as grounds for + noun phrase · passive be cited as · passive be cited for
entries.never: cite that the deal was dead — cite takes a noun phrase, not a that-clause. Repairs: cited the collapse of the deal, cited sources as saying that the deal was dead, or simply said that the deal was dead. It takes no personal object for the hearer either (cited me the ruling ✗ → cited the ruling to me ✓) and no embedded question (cited why the deal died ✗ → cited the reason the deal died ✓).
entries.reports: the source or the reason behind a statement rather than the statement itself. Quote reproduces the words; cite names where they came from or what they support.
entries.see also: quote, paraphrase, indicate, point out, echo

examples: She clarified that the discount applies only to the first order.
Could you clarify what "reasonable notice" means in this contract?
The spokesman clarified the timeline for reporters the next morning.
Let me clarify one thing before we go any further.
The memo was sent out to clarify who signs off on refunds.
He clarified for the committee that no money had actually changed hands.
entries.русский: уточнить, разъяснить — снять двусмысленность уже сказанного, а не восполнить пробел
entries.register: neutral to formal; heavy in business and official speech
entries.type: reporting verb — explanation that removes an ambiguity
entries.patterns: clarify + that-clause · clarify + wh-clause · clarify + whether-clause · clarify + noun phrase · clarify + noun phrase + for sb · clarify + to / for sb + that-clause · passive it was clarified that
entries.never: clarify me the rules — no personal object. The beneficiary takes for far more often than to: Could you clarify that for me? is the natural form, and Could you clarify me that? is not English. Clarify also takes no to-infinitive and no -ing: clarify to be leaving ✗, clarify sending it ✗ → She clarified that she was leaving ✓, He clarified that he had sent it ✓.
entries.reports: a second statement that fixes the meaning of a first one. Explain supplies information that was missing; clarify repairs information that was already there and came out ambiguous. Note what that presupposes: calling something a clarification concedes that the first statement was unclear, which is why officials reach for it when they are walking a remark back without admitting they changed it.
entries.see also: explain, spell out, point out, indicate, reiterate

examples: The board concluded that no policy had been violated.
From the tone of the email I concluded we weren't getting the contract.
Two separate reviews concluded the same thing.
The inspector concluded that the crack was cosmetic.
She concluded her remarks by thanking the outgoing treasurer.
It would be premature to conclude that the trend is permanent.
entries.русский: заключить, прийти к выводу — вывод подан как итог взвешенных доводов
entries.type: reporting verb — judgment reached from evidence
entries.patterns: conclude + that-clause · conclude + from + noun phrase + that-clause · conclude + noun phrase (conclude an agreement — a different sense) · conclude + by + -ing (= finish) · conclude + with + noun phrase (= finish) · passive it was concluded that
entries.never: conclude someone that and conclude to do something — no personal object, and no infinitive in the active. And no wh-clause: conclude what had gone wrong ✗ → She concluded that the seal had failed ✓ or She worked out what had gone wrong ✓. Keep the two senses apart as well: conclude + noun phrase means finish or settle (concluded the meeting, concluded a deal), never decide about — conclude the cause ✗ → He concluded that the cause was electrical ✓.
entries.reports: a judgment presented as the endpoint of reasoning. Assume skips the evidence, speculate offers a guess, conclude claims the evidence has been weighed and the matter settled.
entries.see also: infer, deduce, gather, reason, argue, assume

examples: Consult your doctor before you double the dose.
She consulted two contractors and got two very different numbers.
He consulted the manual, which turned out to be for a different model.
The mayor said she would consult with the council before signing anything.
Nobody consulted the people who actually use the building.
I'd consult an accountant about that if I were you.
entries.русский: консультироваться, обращаться за советом — спросить у знающего или проверить в источнике
entries.type: reporting verb — question put to an authority
entries.patterns: consult + person or reference (consult a lawyer, consult the manual) · consult + sb + about / on + noun phrase · consult + with + sb (standard American) · consult + with + sb + about / on + noun phrase · consult + sb + about + wh-clause · consult + about + noun phrase · passive be consulted about
entries.never: consult to someone and consult me whether the road was open — consult never takes a clause of its own. The question has to ride in on a preposition: consulted the ranger about whether the road was open ✓. It takes no to-infinitive either: consulted him to fix the wiring ✗ → consulted him about the wiring ✓ or asked him to fix the wiring ✓.
entries.reports: asking someone with standing to answer — a professional, a document, a colleague whose agreement you need. Ask is neutral about who is being asked; consult implies expertise or authority on the other end.
entries.see also: ask, inquire, query, question, quiz

examples: From the postmark she deduced that the letter had sat somewhere for a week.
He deduced the password from a photograph of the desk.
You can deduce how old the tree is by counting the rings.
Nothing in the file lets you deduce who authorized the payment.
She deduced, correctly, that the meeting had been canceled without her.
The whole plot depends on a conclusion no reader could possibly deduce.
entries.pronunciation note: American English drops the glide; British di-DYOOSS
entries.русский: вывести, заключить — книжн.: вывод, поданный как необходимо следующий из посылок
entries.type: reporting verb — conclusion drawn by strict inference
entries.patterns: deduce + that-clause · deduce + wh-clause · deduce + noun phrase · deduce + noun phrase + from + noun phrase · deduce + from + noun phrase + that-clause · passive it can be deduced that
entries.never: deduce someone that and deduce to someone — no personal object. Deduce also has no -ing frame and no infinitive: deduce her being there ✗, deduce her to have been there ✗ → He deduced that she had been there ✓.
entries.reports: a conclusion the speaker presents as forced by the premises. Infer leaves room for probability; deduce claims necessity, which is why the detective deduces and the reader infers.
entries.see also: infer, conclude, gather, reason, figure

examples: He demanded to know why his bag had been searched.
Shareholders demanded to know what the severance package cost.
She called back and demanded to know whether the charge had been reversed.
A reporter demanded to know who was paying for the flights.
The parents demanded to know how the school had missed it for two years.
I don't think you're in a position to demand to know anything.
entries.русский: требовать ответа, допытываться — вопрос как претензия: ответ вам якобы должны
entries.register: neutral, but strongly marked for confrontation; common in news writing
entries.type: reporting verb — question asked with force
entries.patterns: demand to know + wh-clause · demand to know + if / whether-clause · demand to know + noun phrase (demand to know the reason) · demand to know + from sb + wh-clause
entries.never: demand me to know and demand to know me why — nothing may come between demand and to know, and no personal object follows. The person addressed rides on a preposition or not at all: She demanded to know from the manager why the account had been frozen ✓. Note also that plain demand + that-clause takes the subjunctive (demanded that he leave), a request rather than a question.
entries.reports: a question asked as a challenge, with the implication that an answer is owed. It is the confrontational end of ask and the exact opposite of the deferential I was wondering.
entries.see also: want to know, ask, question, interrogate, Reported questions

examples: The trial demonstrated that the drug worked no better than a placebo.
She demonstrated to the committee how easily the lock could be picked.
The instructor demonstrated the technique twice before letting anyone try.
These numbers demonstrate what happens when maintenance gets deferred.
Nothing in the audit demonstrates fraud — only sloppiness.
He demonstrated to us that the software had been logging keystrokes.
entries.русский: показать, продемонстрировать — книжн.: доказать наглядно; фактивный глагол
entries.type: reporting verb — proof by showing
entries.patterns: demonstrate + that-clause · demonstrate + wh-clause · demonstrate + noun phrase · demonstrate + to sb + that-clause · demonstrate + to sb + wh-clause · demonstrate + noun phrase + to sb · demonstrate + how / what + to-infinitive · passive it has been demonstrated that
entries.never: demonstrate me how it works — this is the same error as explain me, and it is worth learning as a pair with show, which does take the object: show me how it works ✓, demonstrate to me how it works ✓, demonstrate me how it works ✗. The block holds in front of every complement, so demonstrate the committee that the lock could be picked ✗ → demonstrated to the committee that… ✓. And no -ing: demonstrate the seal failing ✗ → demonstrated that the seal failed ✓.
entries.reports: establishing something by making it visible — an experiment, a walkthrough, a table of results. Show is the everyday word for the same act; demonstrate is its formal counterpart and implies a deliberate display. Both are factive, like point out: write The trial demonstrated that the drug worked and you have stated as your own that the drug worked. If you are only reporting a claim, the verb is said or claimed.
entries.see also: show, prove, explain, indicate, point out

examples: Several council members echoed her concerns about the parking plan.
The governor's statement echoed language used by the industry group almost word for word.
He echoed what the previous speaker had said and sat down.
The review echoes a complaint that shows up in half the ratings.
Her boss echoed the sentiment without committing to anything.
Every op-ed that week echoed the same three talking points.
entries.русский: вторить, повторять за кем-то — чужие слова с согласием; часто с оттенком упрёка
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in journalism
entries.type: reporting verb — repetition of someone else's statement
entries.patterns: echo + noun phrase (echo his words, echo the sentiment) · echo + sb (echoed the senator) · echo + free relative (echoed what she had said) · echo + that-clause (journalistic and marginal — the object is normally a noun phrase)
entries.never: echo to someone that and echo someone that — no hearer slot at all. What is echoed is the object: She echoed his warning, never She echoed us his warning. And echo takes no embedded question: He echoed whether the plan would work ✗, He echoed why she had left ✗. Echoed what she had said ✓ only looks like an exception — that what-clause is a free relative standing in for a noun phrase ("the thing she had said"), not a question. Treat echo + that-clause as journalistic shorthand and prefer echoed the point that… or agreed that… in careful prose.
entries.reports: repeating what someone else has already said, with agreement implied. Repeat says the same words again, possibly your own; echo says someone else's, and takes their side by doing so. It carries a second, quieter judgment as well: an echo adds nothing, so He merely echoed the party line is a criticism in a way that He repeated the party line is not.
entries.see also: repeat, reiterate, quote, paraphrase, cite

examples: (British usage) She enquired about the opening hours of the archive.
(British usage) He enquired whether a table by the window was available.
(British usage) Guests should enquire at the front desk.
In American English, that last sentence would read inquire at the front desk.
The style guide flags enquire and replaces it with inquire automatically.
British firms often label the contact page Enquiries; American ones write Inquiries.
entries.русский: справляться, осведомляться — брит. написание; амер. английский пишет inquire
entries.register: British spelling. American English writes inquire in every sense; enquire in an American document reads as a typo or an affectation
entries.type: reporting verb — question
entries.patterns: identical to inquire — enquire + wh-clause · enquire + if / whether-clause · enquire + about / after / into + noun phrase · enquire + of sb + whether (very formal)
entries.never: enquire me — like inquire, it takes no personal object, and no that-clause either (enquired that the position was open ✗). And in American writing, avoid the spelling itself: use inquire. British usage splits the two by sense — enquire to ask a question, inquire to investigate formally — but that split is not observed in the United States, where inquire covers both. The noun follows the verb: British enquiry, American inquiry.
entries.other british spellings in this territor: enquire is one of a family a learner will meet in the same sources, and every one of them is wrong in an American document — British summarise, apologise, criticise, recognise, emphasise, analyse → American summarize, apologize, criticize, recognize, emphasize, analyze. Two further differences are not spelling at all but grammar: British reckon to do something (I reckon to finish by six) is not American, and British writers use query + wh-clause more freely than American ones do.
entries.reports: exactly what inquire reports: a question asked formally or politely. The entry exists here so the spelling can be recognized in British sources and then not copied.
entries.see also: inquire, ask, query, inquire, not enquire

examples: The contractor estimated that the roof had five years left in it.
Police estimated the crowd at twelve hundred; organizers said four thousand.
Can you estimate how much of the budget goes to overtime?
The damage is estimated at nine million dollars.
She estimated the drive at four hours and was off by two.
Nobody could estimate what the delay would cost.
The appraiser estimated the collection to be worth about sixty thousand dollars.
entries.pronunciation note: ES-tuh-mit — the last vowel is full in the verb and reduced in the noun
entries.русский: оценить, прикинуть — назвать величину как приблизительную (ср. calculate — точный расчёт)
entries.type: reporting verb — approximate figure
entries.patterns: estimate + that-clause · estimate + wh-clause (estimate how many) · estimate + noun phrase · estimate + noun phrase + at + amount · estimate + noun phrase + to be + value (formal: estimated the loss to be four million dollars) · passive be estimated to be / at · passive it is estimated that
entries.never: estimate someone that and estimate me the cost — no personal object in either slot. The infinitive is narrower than it looks: estimate + noun phrase + to be is standard in formal writing (estimated the age of the tree to be two hundred years ✓), but there is no object-less infinitive (estimated to take a week ✗ in the active), and an eventive infinitive reads badly even with an object (estimated repairs to take a week ✗). Say estimated that repairs would take a week ✓.
entries.reports: a number offered as approximate. Calculate claims the figure was derived and is exact; estimate concedes up front that it is not.
entries.see also: calculate, reckon, figure, predict, speculate

examples: She explained that the fee is charged per bag, not per passenger.
Could you explain to me why my account was closed?
He explained the rules twice and half the room still got it wrong.
Nobody ever explained how the two departments were supposed to share the budget.
The label explains what to do if the paint gets on your skin.
I tried to explain the situation to my landlord and got nowhere.
entries.русский: объяснять — не берёт дополнение лица напрямую: explain to me ✓, «explain me» ✗
entries.type: reporting verb — explanation
entries.patterns: explain + that-clause · explain + wh-clause · explain + whether-clause · explain + noun phrase · explain + to sb + that-clause · explain + to sb + wh-clause · explain + noun phrase + to sb · explain + how / what / why + to-infinitive · explain oneself · passive it was explained that
entries.never: explain me something — this is the single most common error in the whole group. Explain takes no personal object before its complement; the hearer must arrive on to. Repairs: explain it to me, explain to me what happened, explain to me that it was an accident. The same block applies to explain me how ✗ → explain to me how ✓. Note that tell and show behave the opposite way (tell me what happened, show me what happened), which is exactly why the error is so persistent. Explain also takes no -ing and no to-infinitive complement: explain losing the file ✗, explain to have lost the file ✗ → He explained that he had lost the file ✓ or He explained how he had lost the file ✓.
entries.word order: when both the hearer and the content are present, the short one goes first. Explain it to me ✓ / explain to me it ✗; but with a full clause the to-phrase leads: He explained to the class why the experiment had failed ✓, and He explained why the experiment had failed to the class is grammatical but reads as though the experiment failed at the class.
entries.reports: supplying the information or the reason that makes something understandable. Say just reports words; explain claims those words answered a why or a how.
entries.see also: clarify, spell out, demonstrate, show, point out, Reported questions

examples: I figured you'd want the window seat.
She figured the store would be closed by the time they got there.
We figured on about an hour of traffic and got two.
He figured her for a reporter the moment she pulled out a notebook.
It took the mechanic ten minutes to figure out what was rattling.
Go ahead and start — we'll figure out who's paying later.
With both starters hurt, the game figures to be low-scoring.
She finally figured out that the two invoices were for the same job.
entries.pronunciation note: American English keeps the y glide; British FIG-uh
entries.русский: прикинуть, смекнуть — разг., амер.: быстрое рабочее предположение; аналог reckon и suppose
entries.type: reporting verb — casual conclusion
entries.patterns: figure + that-clause (the that is nearly always dropped) · figure + sb/sth + for + noun phrase (figured him for a cop) · figure + on + noun phrase · figure + on + -ing · figure + to-infinitive (= be likely to: the game figures to be close) · figure out + wh-clause · figure out + that-clause · figure out + noun phrase · figure + noun phrase + out (separable: figure it out)
entries.never: figure someone that and figure me the answer — no personal object in either slot. Keep figure apart from figure out: plain figure takes a that-clause and reports a guess (I figured he'd be late), while figure out takes a wh-clause and reports a solved problem (I figured out why he was late). figure why he was late is not English. Keep the two to-forms apart as well: X figures to be Y means "is likely to be" and wants a non-personal subject (the game figures to be close ✓), while I figured to leave early meaning "I intended to" is dialectal at best — say I figured I'd leave early ✓. And the particle rule holds: figure it out ✓, figure out it ✗.
entries.reports: a working assumption arrived at quickly and offered without much weight behind it. It is the everyday American equivalent of reckon and suppose, and it is at home in speech and dialogue but not in a report or a brief.
entries.see also: reckon, suppose, gather, assume, think

examples: The service forecast a hard freeze by Thursday morning.
Analysts forecast that the shortage would ease by summer.
She forecasted the same slowdown a year before anyone else did.
Utilities are forecast to raise rates twice in the next two years.
Nobody forecast how quickly the market would turn.
The model forecasts demand district by district.
The budget office forecast the shortfall at just under a billion dollars.
entries.pronunciation note: past tense forecast or forecasted; forecast is preferred in American weather and business usage
entries.русский: прогнозировать — офиц.: прогноз по модели или данным, обычно о числовой величине
entries.type: reporting verb — prediction, usually quantified
entries.patterns: forecast + that-clause · forecast + noun phrase · forecast + wh-clause (forecast how much) · forecast + noun phrase + at + amount (forecast the deficit at two billion) · passive be forecast to · passive it is forecast that
entries.never: forecast someone that and forecast someone to do something — no personal object. And in careful prose forecast takes no to-infinitive in the active: say forecast that sales would rise, not forecast sales to rise. The infinitive frame does surface in financial writing and headlines, but only the passive is fully standard — sales are forecast to rise ✓.
entries.reports: a prediction backed by a model or a method, usually about a measurable quantity. Predict is the general word and covers hunches; forecast implies data behind the number.
entries.see also: predict, estimate, calculate, speculate, assume

examples: I gather you've already spoken to legal about this.
From the silence in the room she gathered that the news was bad.
He gathered the position had been filled weeks earlier.
"They're not coming." — "So I gathered."
From what I gather, the lease runs through next spring.
We gathered from her tone that the conversation was over.
entries.русский: понять, заключить из услышанного — «насколько я понял»: источник не назван
entries.type: reporting verb — secondhand understanding
entries.patterns: gather + that-clause (the that is usually dropped) · gather + from + noun phrase + that-clause · gather + as much / so (So I gathered) · I gather as a parenthetical (You're leaving, I gather)
entries.never: gather someone that and gather to someone — no personal object. Gather also avoids the wh-clause and the -ing: gather where he went ✗, gather him leaving ✗; use the fixed phrase from what I gather instead, or a that-clause.
entries.reports: a belief picked up indirectly, with the source deliberately left vague. I gather you're leaving means someone told me, I am not saying who, and I am giving you room to correct it — which is why it works as a polite opener where I heard would sound like gossip. It also hedges: like understand, it passes the claim along without vouching for it, so the reporter is not on the hook if it turns out to be wrong.
entries.see also: understand, infer, deduce, believe, suppose

examples: The company indicated that layoffs were unlikely before the fall.
Early returns indicate a close race in three counties.
She indicated to her supervisor that she was considering other offers.
Nothing in the file indicates who approved the transfer.
The survey indicates how far behind the district has fallen.
He indicated his willingness to testify without ever quite saying yes.
entries.русский: дать понять; свидетельствовать — офиц.: заявление без обязательства; о данных — указывать
entries.register: formal; heavy in official, legal, and news writing
entries.type: reporting verb — guarded statement or signal
entries.patterns: indicate + that-clause · indicate + wh-clause · indicate + whether-clause · indicate + noun phrase · indicate + to sb + that-clause · indicate + to sb + wh-clause · passive it was indicated that
entries.never: indicate me that and indicate someone something — no personal object; the hearer takes to, as in indicated to reporters that no arrest was imminent. Indicate also takes no to-infinitive in the active and no -ing: indicate to resign ✗, indicate resigning ✗ → He indicated that he would resign ✓.
entries.reports: two things at once, which is why officials love it. With a person as subject it reports a statement the writer does not want to call a promise (He indicated that he would resign: he said something in that direction, and it was not a commitment). With an inanimate subject it reports evidence rather than speech (The data indicate that), where it sits a step below show and demonstrate in confidence.
entries.see also: show, demonstrate, point out, cite, prove, suggest

examples: From his silence I inferred that the answer was no.
Readers were left to infer what the company actually planned to do.
She inferred from the invoice that the work had already been done.
You can't infer causation from a chart like that.
He inferred a threat where none was intended.
What am I supposed to infer from a two-word reply?
entries.русский: сделать вывод — вывод слушателя из сказанного (не путать с imply — «подразумевать»)
entries.type: reporting verb — conclusion drawn by the listener
entries.patterns: infer + that-clause · infer + wh-clause · infer + noun phrase · infer + noun phrase + from + noun phrase · infer + from + noun phrase + that-clause · passive it can be inferred that
entries.never: infer someone that and infer to someone — no personal object, and no -ing (inferred him lying ✗). And do not use infer to mean imply: Are you inferring that I lied? is a very common error for implying. The speaker implies; the listener infers. The mistaken sense is old and widespread in speech, and it is still corrected everywhere it matters, so it is worth keeping straight.
entries.reports: what a hearer concluded from what was said, not what the speaker said. Deduce claims necessity; infer claims only that the conclusion was reasonable.
entries.see also: deduce, conclude, gather, understand, reason

examples: She inquired whether the museum offered a student rate.
He called the office to inquire about the status of his application.
The letter inquires after your mother, which is more than she deserves.
The committee was formed to inquire into the cost overruns.
A guest inquired of the concierge where the nearest pharmacy was.
Several readers have inquired why the column stopped running.
Counsel inquired as to whether the witness had been shown the document beforehand.
entries.русский: осведомляться, справляться — офиц.: то же, что ask, но выше регистром; амер. написание
entries.register: formal. American English uses this spelling in every sense; enquire is British
entries.type: reporting verb — question, formally or politely put
entries.patterns: inquire + wh-clause · inquire + if / whether-clause · inquire + about + noun phrase · inquire + after + person (health) · inquire + into + noun phrase (investigate) · inquire + as to + noun phrase or wh-clause (very formal) · inquire + of sb + whether / wh-clause (very formal) · inquire + direct quotation, as a quotative tag
entries.never: inquire me and inquire the registrar whether — inquire takes no personal object. The person is either dropped or introduced by of: inquired of the registrar whether the position had been filled ✓, or simply use ask: asked the registrar whether… ✓. And no that-clause: inquire that the position was open ✗ — a question verb needs a question, so inquired whether the position was open ✓.
entries.reports: the same act as ask, raised in register. Choosing it signals formality or distance, so in ordinary conversation it can sound stiff or faintly sarcastic (He inquired as to the whereabouts of his sandwich).
entries.see also: enquire, ask, query, consult, Reported questions

examples: He was interrogated for six hours without a lawyer present.
Border agents interrogated her about the purpose of the trip.
The film interrogates the idea that hard work alone explains success.
My mother interrogated me about every friend whose name she didn't recognize.
They interrogated both drivers separately and got the same story.
Nobody interrogated the numbers before they went into the press release.
entries.русский: допрашивать — офиц.: длительный и жёсткий расспрос как процесс, а не отдельный вопрос
entries.type: reporting verb — sustained hostile questioning
entries.patterns: interrogate + person · interrogate + sb + about / on + noun phrase · interrogate + sb + about + wh-clause · interrogate + noun phrase (academic: interrogate the assumption) · passive be interrogated about
entries.never: interrogate whether he was home and interrogate someone something — interrogate cannot take a clause at all. Its object is the person being questioned, and the subject matter arrives on about: interrogated him about where he had been ✓, interrogated where he had been ✗. No that-clause either (interrogate that he had lied ✗) and no double object.
entries.reports: questioning as a process rather than a question. It reports that someone was put under pressure over time, not that one thing was asked, so it never carries the content of a single question the way ask does.
entries.see also: question, quiz, query, demand to know, ask

examples: She paraphrased the ruling for readers who weren't going to read forty pages of it.
I'm paraphrasing, but that was the gist of what he told me.
To paraphrase my grandmother, nothing bought on sale was ever a bargain.
The summary paraphrases three separate reports without citing any of them.
He paraphrased the complaint so gently that it stopped sounding like a complaint.
If you paraphrase a source, you still owe it a footnote.
entries.русский: пересказать своими словами, перефразировать — передать смысл, не сохраняя формулировок
entries.type: reporting verb — restatement in other words
entries.patterns: paraphrase + noun phrase · paraphrase + sb (paraphrase Orwell) · paraphrase + noun phrase + for sb · paraphrase + free relative (paraphrase what he said) · used absolutely (I'm paraphrasing) · to paraphrase + sb, as a sentence adverbial · passive be paraphrased as
entries.never: paraphrase that the policy had changed and paraphrase me the argument — paraphrase takes a noun phrase, not a that-clause and not a double object. Repairs: paraphrased the memo, paraphrased the memo for me, or said, paraphrasing the memo, that the policy had changed. It takes no embedded question either: paraphrased whether the policy had changed ✗.
entries.reports: the content of what someone said, rewritten. It is the honest label for indirect speech itself: a quotation reproduces the words, a paraphrase keeps the meaning and drops the wording, which is why paraphrased material still needs a citation.
entries.see also: quote, summarize, cite, recap, echo

entries.meaning: Write He pointed out that the report was fabricated and you have said the report was fabricated. If you are not prepared to say that, the verb is claimed or alleged.
examples: She pointed out that we'd already paid for the extra night.
Someone finally pointed out to the group that nobody had booked a room.
He pointed out how much cheaper the annual plan works out to be.
It's worth pointing out that the rule has never once been enforced.
I pointed the discrepancy out to accounting and heard nothing back.
As critics point out, the survey never asked people who had left.
She pointed out to the new hires exactly where the process breaks down.
entries.русский: указать, обратить внимание на — фактивный: и говорящий, и пишущий считают это фактом
entries.type: reporting verb — statement of a fact the speaker treats as true
entries.patterns: point out + that-clause · point out + wh-clause · point out + noun phrase · point out + to sb + that-clause · point out + to sb + wh-clause · point + noun phrase + out + to sb (separable with a noun object: point the error out to him) · passive it should be pointed out that
entries.never: point out me that and point me out that — no personal object in either slot. The hearer takes to: pointed out to me that the deadline had passed ✓. Note the particle rule: a pronoun object must sit inside the verb (point it out, never point out it), but a that-clause never can (point that the deadline had passed out ✗). And no -ing or infinitive complement: pointed out him being late ✗, pointed out to be late ✗.
entries.reports: drawing attention to something the speaker takes to be a fact — and, crucially, that the reporter also takes to be a fact. This is the presupposition that separates it from claim:
entries.see also: indicate, explain, clarify, show, argue, prove

examples: He predicted that the bill would die in committee, and it did.
Every forecaster predicted a mild winter.
She predicted what the landlord would say almost word for word.
The storm is predicted to weaken before it reaches the coast.
Nobody predicted how fast the neighborhood would change.
I'm not going to predict the outcome of a case I haven't read.
entries.русский: предсказывать, предрекать — утверждение о будущем, за которое говорящий отвечает
entries.type: reporting verb — statement about the future
entries.patterns: predict + that-clause · predict + wh-clause · predict + whether-clause · predict + noun phrase · passive be predicted to · passive it is predicted that
entries.never: predict someone that and predict me the outcome — no personal object. Predict someone to win turns up in sports and betting writing but is not standard elsewhere; use predicted that she would win. And no -ing: predicted the bill dying in committee ✗ → predicted that the bill would die in committee ✓.
entries.backshift: the will inside a prediction becomes would under a past reporting verb — "It will rain," he predicted → He predicted that it would rain — and would is what makes the prediction read as still open rather than already settled.
entries.reports: a claim about what is going to happen. Forecast implies a model; speculate admits a guess; predict sits between them and commits the speaker.
entries.see also: forecast, speculate, estimate, calculate, assume

examples: The receipts prove that the payment cleared in March.
Nothing in the record proves intent.
She set out to prove to the board that the process could be automated.
He proved everyone wrong within a season.
The rumor proved to be false, though it took a month to die.
You can't prove a negative, as the saying goes.
She proved herself capable of running the department in about six weeks.
Two of the three signatures were later proved to be forgeries.
entries.pronunciation note: past participle proved or proven; American English prefers proved as a verb (has proved) and proven as an adjective (a proven method)
entries.русский: доказать — самое сильное в группе: вопрос закрыт; фактивный глагол
entries.type: reporting verb — demonstration that settles a question
entries.patterns: prove + that-clause · prove + wh-clause (prove who did it) · prove + noun phrase · prove + to sb + that-clause · prove + to sb + wh-clause · prove + noun phrase + adjective (prove him wrong) · prove + noun phrase + noun phrase (prove him a liar) · prove + noun phrase + to be (proved the claim to be false) · prove + reflexive + adjective (proved herself capable) · prove + to-infinitive (= turn out: proved to be false) · passive it has been proved / proven that
entries.never: prove me that it works — the hearer takes to: prove to me that it works ✓. The one place a bare object is fine is the object-complement frame, which is a different structure entirely: prove me wrong ✓, prove him a liar ✓ — there the noun phrase is what is being characterized, not the person being told. And no -ing complement: proved him taking the money ✗ → proved that he had taken the money ✓.
entries.reports: the strongest claim in the group — that the matter is now beyond dispute. Argue offers reasons, demonstrate makes something visible, prove asserts the question is closed, so a careful writer reserves it for cases where it really is. It is fully factive: The receipts prove that the payment cleared states, in the reporter's own voice, that the payment cleared.
entries.see also: demonstrate, show, argue, indicate, conclude

examples: She queried the shipping charge and had it removed.
The copy editor queried two dates and a spelling.
Several members queried whether the vote had been properly noticed.
He queried the bank about a withdrawal he didn't recognize.
Nobody queried the figure until the audit, eight months later.
If anything looks off, query it before the file goes to print.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˈkwɛri/ KWAIR-ee in some American speech
entries.русский: поставить под сомнение, запросить уточнение — офиц.: вопрос с подозрением на ошибку
entries.type: reporting verb — question that challenges
entries.patterns: query + noun phrase (query a charge) · query + whether-clause · query + wh-clause (queried why the charge appeared twice — commoner in British writing) · query + sb + about / on + noun phrase · query + direct quotation (fiction: "Are you sure?" he queried) · passive be queried
entries.never: query to someone and query me the total — no double object and no to. No clause after a personal object either: query me whether the total was right ✗ → She queried whether the total was right ✓ or She asked me whether the total was right ✓. And no that-clause: query that the figures were correct ✗ → He queried whether the figures were correct ✓. Also avoid query as a plain substitute for ask in narrative: "What time is it?" he queried reads as amateur fiction, and asked is the word. The verb is in general commoner in British than American English, where question and ask about carry most of this load.
entries.reports: raising a question about whether something is correct. Ask seeks information; query signals suspicion that there is an error, which is why an editor queries a line and a customer queries a charge.
entries.see also: question, ask, inquire, clarify, Reported questions

examples: Police questioned three witnesses at the scene.
She questioned whether the committee had the authority to do that.
Reporters questioned the mayor about the missing emails for twenty minutes.
Nobody questioned the budget until it was already approved.
He questioned why the same vendor kept winning every contract.
I don't question her motives — only her arithmetic.
Nobody questions that the program works; the argument is over what it costs.
entries.русский: допрашивать, расспрашивать (о человеке); ставить под сомнение (о деле или с whether)
entries.type: reporting verb — sustained questioning, or expressed doubt
entries.patterns: question + person · question + sb + about / on + noun phrase · question + noun phrase (question the decision) · question + whether / if-clause · question + wh-clause (question how / question why) · question + that-clause, chiefly under negation (I don't question that she meant well) · passive be questioned about
entries.never: question me the details — no double object; the topic takes about: questioned me about the details ✓. And the two senses do not mix their frames: with a person object it means interrogate (They questioned him for an hour), with a thing object or a whether-clause it means doubt (She questioned the timing, She questioned whether it was legal). question him whether he had been there ✗ → asked him whether… ✓. Watch the that-clause: it is fine under negation (Nobody questions that the policy works ✓) but odd in the affirmative — question that the vote was legal ✗ → She questioned whether the vote was legal ✓. And question + wh-clause raises a challenge rather than reporting an act of asking: He questioned why the same vendor kept winning means he was calling it into doubt, not that he put the question to somebody.
entries.reports: either the act of putting questions to someone, or the act of casting doubt. Which one you get is decided entirely by what follows the verb, so the frame carries the meaning here more than the word does.
entries.see also: interrogate, query, quiz, ask, demand to know

examples: Reporters quizzed the coach about his starting lineup.
She quizzed me on vocabulary the whole way to school.
He got quizzed about the gap in his résumé at every interview.
The kids quizzed their grandfather about what the town used to look like.
Nobody quizzed him too hard about where the money came from.
I quizzed the salesman on the warranty until he gave up and got the manager.
entries.русский: расспрашивать, засыпать вопросами — разг.: настойчиво и любопытно, но не враждебно
entries.register: informal; also a staple of headline and tabloid writing
entries.type: reporting verb — persistent questioning
entries.patterns: quiz + sb · quiz + sb + about / on + noun phrase · quiz + sb + about / on + wh-clause · passive be quizzed about / on
entries.never: quiz whether the flight was on time and quiz someone something — like interrogate, quiz takes a person as its object and never a clause of its own. Repairs: quizzed her about the flight, asked whether the flight was on time. No that-clause either (quiz that the flight was late ✗), and no to: quiz to her about it ✗.
entries.reports: questioning that is repeated and a little pushy, but not hostile — a parent, a teacher, or a reporter working through a list. Where interrogate is grim, quiz is closer to nosy.
entries.see also: question, interrogate, query, ask, demand to know

examples: She quoted the lease back to him, clause and line number.
The story quotes two neighbors who heard the argument.
He was widely quoted as saying the plan was dead on arrival.
Don't quote me on the exact figure — I'd have to look it up.
The professor quoted from a letter nobody knew existed.
The dealer quoted us four thousand dollars for the same repair.
entries.русский: цитировать, приводить дословно — точные слова говорящего, с ручательством за точность
entries.type: reporting verb — reproduction of exact words
entries.patterns: quote + noun phrase (quote the statute, quote his exact words) · quote + sb · quote + sb + as saying (+ that-clause) · quote + sb + on + noun phrase (don't quote me on that) · quote + noun phrase + to sb · quote + from + noun phrase · quote + sb + amount (quote me a price — a different sense) · passive be quoted as saying
entries.never: quoted him that the deal was off — quote cannot take a bare that-clause after a person. The journalistic frame is fixed: quoted him as saying that the deal was off ✓. There is no embedded question either (quote him whether the deal was off ✗), and the only double-object frame belongs to the pricing sense (quote me a price ✓, quote me the statute ✗ → quote the statute to me ✓). And do not use quote for a paraphrase: if the words are not the speaker's own, the verb is paraphrase or say.
entries.reports: the speaker's actual wording, presented as verbatim. That is the whole distinction — say reports content, quote reports the words themselves and puts the reporter on the hook for their accuracy.
entries.see also: cite, paraphrase, echo, repeat, Punctuating direct speech

examples: He reasoned that a second key had to exist somewhere in the house.
She reasoned that nobody would check the file until Monday.
"They'd have called by now," he reasoned.
The committee reasoned that a smaller pilot carried less risk.
I reasoned that the fastest route was also the one everyone else would take.
You can't reason with someone who has already decided.
entries.русский: рассуждать, заключить — книжн./повествоват.: вывод вместе с ходом мысли, про себя
entries.register: neutral to literary; most at home in narrative
entries.type: reporting verb — conclusion presented with its reasoning
entries.patterns: reason + that-clause · reason + direct quotation, as a quotative tag ("He must have missed the exit," she reasoned.) · reason + from + noun phrase (+ to + noun phrase) · reason + about + noun phrase (formal, in logic and philosophy) · reason out + noun phrase or wh-clause · reason + with + person (a different verb: try to persuade)
entries.never: reason someone that and reason to do something — no personal object, no infinitive. And no bare wh-clause: reason why the door stuck ✗ → He reasoned that the door stuck because the frame had swollen ✓ or He reasoned out why the door stuck ✓. Keep reason that apart from reason with: She reasoned that he was lying reports a conclusion; She reasoned with him reports an attempt to talk him around, and takes no clause at all.
entries.reports: a conclusion together with the thinking behind it, usually silent. It is the narrator's verb — he reasoned labels a line of thought the reader is being shown, which is why it appears far more often in fiction than in conversation.
entries.see also: conclude, infer, deduce, argue, figure

examples: Let me recap where we landed before everybody scatters.
She recapped the first two episodes for anyone joining late.
He recapped what each department had committed to.
To recap: the deposit is refundable, the fee is not.
The blog recaps every game in about four hundred words.
Nobody wanted to sit through another recap of the same argument.
entries.pronunciation note: REE-kap — doubles the p: recapped, recapping
entries.русский: кратко повторить, резюмировать — разг.: пробежаться по уже пройденному по порядку
entries.register: informal to neutral; standard in meetings, sports, and broadcasting
entries.type: reporting verb — brief restatement of what was already covered
entries.patterns: recap + noun phrase · recap + wh-clause · recap + noun phrase + for sb · recap + for sb · to recap, as a sentence adverbial · used absolutely (Let me recap)
entries.never: recap that the deadline had moved and recap me the meeting — no that-clause and no double object. Repairs: recapped the decision, recapped the meeting for me, recapped what had been decided. The beneficiary takes for, never to: recapped the meeting to me ✗.
entries.reports: a short replay of ground already covered, for people who were there or who just arrived. Summarize condenses a body of material; recap replays a sequence of events or points in order.
entries.see also: summarize, repeat, reiterate, paraphrase, spell out

examples: I reckon we'll be there by six if the traffic holds.
He reckoned the truck had another winter in it.
"Think it'll rain?" — "I reckon so."
She reckoned the cost of the repair at about half what the shop quoted.
The bridge is reckoned to be the oldest still in use in the county.
Nobody around here reckons much of the new zoning plan.
The county assessor is a force to be reckoned with, whatever you think of her.
entries.русский: полагать, считать — разг., диал.: южное и сельское амер.; в формальном письме неуместно
entries.register: informal. In American English it is regional — ordinary in Southern and rural speech, and elsewhere either jocular or a bit of borrowed British
entries.type: reporting verb — casual opinion or rough calculation
entries.patterns: reckon + that-clause (the that is nearly always dropped) · reckon + noun phrase (reckon the cost — the older "calculate" sense) · reckon + noun phrase + at + amount · reckon + sb/sth + to be (mostly passive: is reckoned to be) · reckon + so / not · reckon + with + noun phrase (a different sense, = deal with: a force to be reckoned with) · reckon + on + noun phrase or -ing (chiefly British)
entries.never: reckon someone that — no personal object, and no wh-clause (reckon where he went ✗). And in American English avoid reckon to do something meaning "expect to," which is a British and dialectal frame: say I reckon I'll head out ✓, not I reckon to head out ✗. Reckon on is British too — an American says counted on or figured on.
entries.reports: an opinion held loosely and offered without ceremony. Think is the neutral version; reckon adds a regional and conversational color that will be heard, so it does not belong in formal writing.
entries.see also: figure, suppose, think, estimate, calculate

examples: He reiterated that the deadline would not move under any circumstances.
The company reiterated its guidance for the fourth quarter.
She reiterated to the staff that nobody's job was at risk.
The court reiterated a principle it had already stated twice that term.
Let me reiterate one point, because it got lost the first time.
I've reiterated this in three separate emails.
entries.русский: вновь заявить, повторить настойчиво — офиц.: намеренный повтор, чтобы снять сомнения
entries.type: reporting verb — deliberate restatement
entries.patterns: reiterate + that-clause · reiterate + noun phrase (reiterate his support, reiterate the offer) · reiterate + free relative (reiterated what she had said in June) · reiterate + to sb + that-clause · passive it was reiterated that
entries.never: reiterate me that and reiterate someone the offer — no personal object. No embedded question either: reiterated whether the deadline would move ✗ → reiterated that the deadline would not move ✓. And avoid reiterate again: re- already carries the repetition, so the again is redundant — a mistake common enough in business writing that editors flag it on sight.
entries.reports: saying the same thing a second time on purpose, to close off doubt. Repeat is neutral about why; reiterate implies the first statement was not accepted or not heard, which is why it turns up in press briefings more than anywhere else.
entries.see also: repeat, echo, clarify, spell out, recap

examples: He repeated that he had never met the man.
Could you repeat the last part? The line cut out.
She repeated the instructions slowly, one step at a time.
Don't repeat any of this to your brother.
The witness repeated what she had told police the night before.
The teacher had the class repeat each phrase after her.
entries.русский: повторить — своё или чужое; без согласия (ср. echo) и без дословности (ср. quote)
entries.type: reporting verb — restatement, one's own or someone else's
entries.patterns: repeat + that-clause · repeat + noun phrase · repeat + free relative (repeat what he said) · repeat + direct quotation · repeat + noun phrase + to sb · repeat + noun phrase + for sb · repeat oneself · repeat + after sb · passive be repeated
entries.never: repeat me the question — no double object. The hearer takes to or for: repeat the question for me ✓, repeat it to the class ✓. No embedded question either — repeat whether he had met the man ✗ → He repeated that he had never met the man ✓; repeat what he said ✓ is a free relative, not a question. Repeat again is redundant in the same way as reiterate again, though it is far more common in speech and rarely worth correcting there.
entries.reports: saying something over — either restating your own point or passing along someone else's words. Unlike echo, it implies no agreement, and unlike quote, it does not promise the wording is exact.
entries.see also: reiterate, echo, recap, quote, clarify

examples: The receipts show that the shipment left on the ninth.
She showed me exactly where the pipe was leaking.
Every study on this shows the same pattern.
He showed the inspector how the alarm had been bypassed.
Let me show you what happens when you click the second tab.
The photos show what the building looked like before the fire.
entries.pronunciation note: past participle shown; showed also occurs and is accepted, though shown is standard in careful American writing
entries.русский: показать; свидетельствовать — берёт дополнение лица (show me), в отличие от explain
entries.type: reporting verb — demonstration or evidence
entries.patterns: show + that-clause · show + wh-clause · show + whether-clause · show + sb + that-clause · show + sb + wh-clause · show + sb + noun phrase · show + noun phrase + to sb · show + sb + wh-word + to-infinitive (show me what to do, show me how to reset it) · passive it has been shown that
entries.never: show to me how it works as a substitute for the double object — show is one of the verbs that does take a personal object directly, so show me how it works is the natural form. Use to only when the thing shown comes first: showed the photo to me ✓, showed me the photo ✓, showed to me the photo ✗. And keep the -ing frame out of reports: showed him leaving the building is perception, not a report of anything said or established — for a report, showed that he had left the building ✓.
entries.reports: making something evident, either by displaying it or by supplying evidence for it. Learn it as the counterweight to explain and demonstrate: show me ✓, explain to me ✓, explain me ✗ — same meaning territory, opposite object rules. Like prove and demonstrate it is factive: Every study shows the same pattern asserts the pattern in the reporter's own voice.
entries.see also: demonstrate, prove, explain, indicate, point out

examples: Analysts speculated that the merger had fallen apart over price.
She refused to speculate about an investigation she wasn't part of.
Neighbors speculated for weeks about who had bought the place.
I don't want to speculate on motives without more information.
The article speculates that a second site was under consideration.
It's pointless to speculate about what he would have wanted.
The memo speculates as to which of the three sites the company actually preferred.
entries.русский: строить догадки — предположение, прямо заявленное как догадка, без доказательств
entries.type: reporting verb — guess offered as a guess
entries.patterns: speculate + that-clause · speculate + about / on + noun phrase · speculate + about / on + wh-clause · speculate + about / on + whether-clause · speculate + as to + wh-clause or noun phrase (formal) · passive it was speculated that
entries.never: speculate someone that and speculate what happened — no personal object, and no bare wh-clause: the question needs a preposition. Repairs: speculated about what had happened ✓, speculated that the roof had failed ✓. No to-infinitive either: speculated the roof to have failed ✗. Keep this sense apart from the financial one, which takes in or on and a market (speculated in currencies).
entries.reports: a possibility floated without evidence, and labeled as such. It is the weakest claim in this group: conclude says the evidence settles it, predict commits the speaker, speculate explicitly declines to.
entries.see also: predict, assume, suppose, wonder, conclude

examples: The email spelled out exactly what would happen if the balance went unpaid.
She spelled out the terms twice, and he signed anyway.
Do I have to spell it out for you?
The policy never spells out who is responsible for the deductible.
He spelled out that no exceptions would be made, for anyone, ever.
Somebody needs to spell the consequences out before the vote.
entries.русский: разжевать, изложить открытым текстом — сказать прямо то, что было лишь подразумеваемо
entries.type: reporting verb — explanation made explicit
entries.patterns: spell out + noun phrase · spell out + that-clause · spell out + wh-clause · spell + noun phrase + out (separable) · spell out + noun phrase + for sb · passive be spelled out
entries.never: spell out me the terms and spell out it — no personal object, and a pronoun object must go inside the verb: spell it out ✓, spell out it ✗. The hearer takes for: spell it out for me ✓. A full noun phrase may go either side (spell out the terms / spell the terms out), but a that-clause always follows the whole verb (spelled out that the fee was nonrefundable).
entries.reports: stating in plain, unmissable terms something that was implied or left vague. Explain fills a gap in the hearer's knowledge; spell out removes the hearer's room to pretend not to have understood.
entries.see also: clarify, explain, point out, reiterate, demonstrate

examples: She summarized the forty-page filing in a single paragraph.
Could you summarize what the consultants actually recommended?
The abstract summarizes the study for readers who won't get past page one.
He summarized the debate so fairly that both sides complained.
To summarize: we're over budget and behind schedule.
The minutes summarize every motion but record no discussion.
entries.pronunciation note: spelled -ize in American English; British summarise
entries.русский: резюмировать, кратко изложить — свести материал к главному для тех, кто его не знает
entries.type: reporting verb — condensed restatement
entries.patterns: summarize + noun phrase · summarize + wh-clause · summarize + noun phrase + for sb · summarize + noun phrase + in + noun phrase (summarized the report in three findings) · summarize + by + -ing · used absolutely (Let me summarize) · to summarize, as a sentence adverbial · passive be summarized as
entries.never: summarize me the report — no double object; the beneficiary takes for: summarize the report for me ✓, while summarize the report to me ✗ is not idiomatic. A that-clause is also a poor fit (He summarized that the project was over budget); use summarized the findings or shift to concluded that if a judgment is what you mean.
entries.reports: compressing a body of material into its main points. Recap replays events in order for people who were present; summarize boils down content for people who were not.
entries.see also: recap, paraphrase, conclude, clarify, repeat

examples: I suppose we could push the meeting to Thursday.
She supposed the noise was just the furnace again.
"Is he any good?" — "I suppose so."
I don't suppose you'd know where the circuit breaker is?
Suppose the flight is canceled — what then?
You're supposed to check in an hour early for international flights.
entries.русский: полагать, допускать — мнение без уверенности, вроде «наверное»; оставляет место возражению
entries.type: reporting verb — tentative belief
entries.patterns: suppose + that-clause · suppose + sb/sth + to-infinitive (chiefly passive: is supposed to be) · imperative suppose (that)… introducing a hypothesis · suppose so / suppose not · passive it is supposed that
entries.never: suppose someone that and suppose to do something in the active — no personal object at all, and I suppose to leave early ✗ is a mangling of the passive idiom I'm supposed to leave early ✓. And no wh-clause and no -ing: suppose where he went ✗, suppose him leaving ✗.
entries.negative raising: I don't suppose usually negates the inner clause, not the supposing — I don't suppose you know his number means "I suppose you don't," and in practice it is a soft request: it is the politest way in American English to ask for something you expect to be refused.
entries.reports: a belief held without much conviction and offered with a shrug. Assume takes it as settled and moves on; suppose leaves it open and half-invites disagreement.
entries.see also: assume, think, believe, reckon, figure, gather

examples: I think the paperwork went out on Monday.
She thought the whole thing was a misunderstanding.
He's thought to be the largest single donor.
I don't think anyone actually read the terms.
Nobody thought to check whether the door locked behind them.
Think what this place would look like with the walls knocked out.
entries.pronunciation note: the n is the -ng sound, not the n of thin
entries.русский: думать, считать — самый частый и наименее обязывающий глагол мнения
entries.register: neutral; the default hedge on any statement
entries.type: reporting verb — opinion or belief; also unspoken thought
entries.patterns: think + that-clause (the that is usually dropped) · think + sb/sth + to be (formal, chiefly passive: is thought to be) · think + noun phrase + adjective (think it odd) · think + of / about + noun phrase · think + about / of + -ing · think + to-infinitive (= remember to: didn't think to ask) · think + wh-clause, exclamative or deliberative only (Think what that would mean, I'm still thinking what to say) · think so / think not · passive it is thought that
entries.never: think someone that and think to me that — no personal object and no hearer slot. Think also does not report a question: think where he had gone ✗ → I wondered where he had gone ✓; the wh-clause it does take is exclamative or deliberative, not an embedded question. Note also that think to do something means "remember to," not "intend to": I didn't think to ask ✓ means the question never occurred to me.
entries.negative raising: I don't think he's coming means I think he isn't coming — the negative attaches to the reporting verb but is understood inside the clause, and this is the ordinary way to say it. I think he isn't coming is grammatical but sounds oddly emphatic, and the tag question follows the inner clause: I don't think he's coming, is he?
entries.reports: an opinion the speaker will not claim to be certain of. It is the least committed of the everyday belief verbs and the most common by a wide margin.
entries.see also: believe, suppose, figure, reckon, gather, assume

examples: I understand the building changed hands last month.
We understand that no charges have been filed.
She understood the deposit to be refundable, and it wasn't.
It is understood that the two sides met privately on Tuesday.
I understand why they did it; I just don't agree with it.
Am I right in understanding that the fee covers both years?
entries.русский: слышать, знать по слухам — «насколько мне известно», без ручательства за источник
entries.register: neutral to formal; a staple of careful journalism and polite business writing
entries.type: reporting verb — belief acquired from an unnamed source
entries.patterns: understand + that-clause · understand + wh-clause · understand + noun phrase · understand + from + noun phrase + that-clause (I understand from your letter that…) · understand + sb/sth + to be (formal: I understood him to be the owner) · passive it is understood that
entries.never: understand me that and understand to someone — no personal object in the reporting sense. (Understand me exists, but it is an imperative meaning "grasp what I am telling you," not a hearer slot.) No -ing either: understand him leaving ✗ → I understand that he is leaving ✓ or I understand why he left ✓.
entries.reports: something the speaker has been told and is passing on without vouching for it or naming who said it. I understand the office is closing means "I have heard this from somewhere I consider reliable" — it hedges the claim and protects the source at the same time, which is exactly why reporters use it.
entries.see also: gather, believe, infer, think, assume

examples: Your sister wants to know what time we're eating.
He wanted to know whether the warranty covered water damage.
The client wants to know why the invoice went up by four hundred dollars.
I want to know who signed off on this.
She wanted to know about the school district before making an offer.
Everybody wants to know how much it costs and nobody wants to ask.
entries.pronunciation note: in running speech want to reduces to wanna: /ˈwɑnə/
entries.русский: хотеть знать — вопрос, передаваемый вживую: наст. вр., без сдвига времён
entries.type: reporting verb — question, often relayed live
entries.patterns: want to know + wh-clause · want to know + if / whether-clause · want to know + noun phrase (want to know the reason) · want to know + about + noun phrase · want to know + from sb + wh-clause
entries.never: want to know me why and want me to know why as a report — the first has no object slot at all, and the second is a different sentence entirely (it reports a wish about what you should know). The person asked takes from: She wanted to know from the manager why the account was frozen ✓.
entries.reports: a question, usually one being relayed to the person who can answer it. Because the reporting verb is often in the present tense (She wants to know…), nothing backshifts, and the report reads as live: She wants to know whether you're free keeps the present because the question is still open.
entries.see also: demand to know, ask, wonder, inquire, Present-tense reporting verbs

examples: I wondered why the lights were still on at two in the morning.
She wondered whether she'd left the stove on, and turned the car around.
He wondered what to say to someone he hadn't spoken to in fifteen years.
We all wondered about the second signature on the form.
It makes you wonder how many other files are missing.
I was wondering if you could take a look at this before Friday.
I don't wonder that she left, after the way that meeting went. (literary — "I'm not surprised")
entries.русский: задаваться вопросом, гадать — вопрос про себя, не вслух (ср. ask — сказано вслух)
entries.type: reporting verb — unspoken question
entries.patterns: wonder + if / whether-clause · wonder + wh-clause · wonder + whether + to-infinitive · wonder + wh-word + to-infinitive (wonder what to do) · wonder + about + noun phrase · wonder + at + noun phrase (= marvel, literary) · wonder + that-clause (= be surprised that — literary: I don't wonder that she left)
entries.never: wonder if to wait — only whether may stand in front of a to-infinitive: wondered whether to wait ✓, wondered if to wait ✗. Also wonder me and wonder someone whether — no personal object, since nothing was said to anybody. And keep statement order inside the clause: I wondered where was he ✗ → I wondered where he was ✓. Do not use the that-clause to report a question: He wondered that she was home does not mean he asked himself whether she was home — it means, in a literary register, that he was surprised she was home. For the question, He wondered whether she was home ✓.
entries.reports: a question the speaker asked themselves and did not say out loud. The contrast with ask is real and worth preserving: He asked whether she was home means he spoke; He wondered whether she was home means he did not.
entries.the polite formula: I was wondering if… is not a report at all — it is a softened request, and the past continuous is doing the softening. I was wondering if you had a minute is a question about now, ends in a period, and expects an answer.
entries.see also: ask, speculate, want to know, inquire, think, Reported questions
